recommendations.source_detail: agent_discovered, ref=2: executor off-heap memory reached 100% utilisation (1.28GB observed vs ~953MB default ceiling derived from executor.memory=9.53GB). Exhausting off-heap overhead causes container kill without clean JVM OOM on Databricks.
recommendations.rationale: The executor's off-heap region is fully saturated: 1.28GB observed usage against an estimated default ceiling of ~953MB (max(384MB, 9.53GB × 10%)). The parameter is not set at all (source=not_set), meaning the runtime default is the only guard. Any increase in reference table scan volume or concurrent shuffle buffers could push this over the limit and cause silent container death — the hardest class of Spark failure to diagnose. Setting memoryOverhead to 1536m provides ~20% headroom over the observed 1.28GB peak. The suggested value follows the guidance of at least 1.5GB from the insight, rounded to a clean 1536m (1.5GB) boundary. This is a stability fix; the marginal memory cost is small relative to the risk of undiagnosed executor kills.
recommendations.explanation: Both `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` and the source confirm this parameter is entirely unset (source=not_set), meaning the runtime's sole guard is the computed default of max(384MB, 9.53GB × 10%) ≈ 953MB. The current run reports an `off_heap_headroom` of exactly 0.0, indicating observed off-heap usage has reached that default ceiling — ~1.28GB against a ~953MB allowance. Because the OS kills the executor process silently when native memory is exhausted, this condition is one of the hardest Spark failure modes to diagnose; setting `memoryOverhead` explicitly to 1536m provides roughly 20% headroom (~256MB) above the 1.28GB observed peak.
recommendations.expected_impact: Eliminates the risk of silent, undiagnosed executor container kills caused by off-heap memory exhaustion, improving run stability without meaningfully increasing cluster cost.
recommendations.risk_note: If the cluster instance type (r6gd.large) has a hard container memory ceiling below heap + 1536m overhead (~11264m total), the executor may be rejected at launch; validate that the total container memory budget accommodates this increase before deploying.

recommendations.source_detail: agent_discovered, ref=2: executor.memory is not explicitly set; the insight derives 9.53GB from the r6gd.large instance. Explicitly pinning it ensures the overhead calculation is anchored to a known value rather than instance-type inference.
recommendations.rationale: The insight shows executor.memory is inferred at ~9.53GB from the r6gd.large instance rather than being explicitly configured. Pinning it explicitly at 9728m (~9.5GB, consistent with current effective value) ensures the overhead reservation computed by the runtime is stable and predictable regardless of cluster topology changes. This pairs with the memoryOverhead fix: with both values explicit the operator can reason about total container memory (9728m heap + 1536m overhead = ~11264m) when sizing the cluster. No heap change is being made — gc_pressure is 0.028 (well below 0.10 threshold) and memory_headroom is 0.55 — this is purely a configuration-hygiene complement to the overhead fix.
recommendations.explanation: Currently `spark.executor.memory` is also not explicitly set (source=not_set), so the effective heap size of ~9.53GB is inferred by the runtime from the r6gd.large instance profile rather than being declared in the Spark conf. Pinning it explicitly at 9728m (~9.5GB) — consistent with the current effective value — makes the overhead formula `max(384MB, 9728m × 10%)` deterministic and stable: any future cluster topology change (instance type swap, Databricks runtime upgrade) can no longer silently shift the effective heap and therefore shift the overhead ceiling. This pairs directly with recommendation #1: with both `spark.executor.memory=9728m` and `spark.executor.memoryOverhead=1536m` declared, total container memory is an explicit, auditable 11264m rather than a runtime inference.
recommendations.expected_impact: Locks in a stable, predictable heap-plus-overhead memory layout so that future cluster or runtime changes cannot inadvertently tighten the off-heap ceiling and reintroduce the exhaustion risk addressed in recommendation #1.

blocked_recommendations.source_detail: agent_discovered, ref=1: 67 shuffle tasks execute sequentially on a single 2-vCore executor per batch; reducing partition count cuts scheduling overhead on each of the 35 batches.
blocked_recommendations.rationale: The insight identifies a 67-task fan-out stage executing on a single executor with only 2 vCores. With cluster_workers=1 and executor_cores=2, the executor can run at most 2 tasks in parallel, meaning 67 partitions requires ~34 sequential rounds per batch. AQE's autoOptimizeShuffle is explicitly false (dbx_autooptimize_shuffle=False) and shuffle_partitions_param='auto' (AQE coalesce) — so AQE may coalesce at runtime, but evidently 67 tasks are still being dispatched in the stage events. Explicitly setting shuffle.partitions to 10 (5× executor_cores, consistent with the rule that ratio > 5 avoids hot-partition risk while ratio < 200 avoids straggler accumulation) reduces per-batch task scheduling rounds from ~34 to ~5, cutting coordination overhead. This is a fine-tuning change and does not conflict with the Tier 1 health fixes. Note: if AQE coalesce is already active and overriding this, the recommendation is a safety net with no regression risk.
blocked_by: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions is set to 'auto' — AQE controls partition count at runtime. Set a fixed numeric value to enable tuning.

unactioned_insights.title: Streaming commitBatch dominates batch latency — Delta checkpoint writes are the bottleneck
unactioned_insights.description: In each micro-batch, the `commitBatch` phase accounts for an average of 15,110ms vs only 3,537ms for `addBatch` (the actual data processing). The commit phase is ~4.3× more expensive than the compute work. This indicates that Delta Lake checkpoint/WAL commit operations — writing offsets and transaction logs — are the rate-limiting step for this streaming query, not CPU or shuffle. With 35 batches over 4.4 hours (avg ~450s/batch), roughly 75% of each batch's wall time is spent on coordination overhead rather than processing. This pattern is exacerbated by the extremely low throughput (0.055 rows/sec input, 1,748 total output rows), meaning the per-row overhead of Delta commits is enormous relative to the data volume processed.
unactioned_insights.reason: The commitBatch dominance insight (ref=0) recommends either (a) increasing the streaming trigger interval (processingTime) or (b) tuning delta.checkpointInterval — neither of which maps to any valid config_key in the allowed set. The insight also recommends evaluating a batch-job architecture, which is a code-level / pipeline-design change, not a Spark parameter change. Skipped: no matching config_key available for trigger interval or Delta checkpoint interval; the architectural suggestion requires code changes outside the scope of Spark config recommendations.

agent_insights.identifier: Massive shuffle-to-output amplification: 5.3GB shuffle to produce 1.05MB output
agent_insights.title: Massive shuffle-to-output amplification: 5.3GB shuffle to produce 1.05MB output
agent_insights.description: Each micro-batch reads ~247K records from a large reference/lookup table and shuffles ~147MB per batch (across 35 batches = ~5.3GB total shuffle) to ultimately write only 1,748 output rows (1.05MB). The shuffle:output ratio is approximately 5,000:1. Stage events show every batch executes a 5-task stage scanning ~247K parquet records via `HashPartitioning(coalesce(add_path_canonical, remove_path_canonical))` followed by a 67-task fan-out stage. The reference dataset (~247K rows, ~1.8GB parquet cache) is being re-scanned and re-shuffled from scratch on every micro-batch rather than being cached or broadcast. With only 2 vCores available and one executor, executing 67 tasks sequentially per batch is also highly serialised.
agent_insights.evidence: shuffle_bytes_read = 5,276,500,518 bytes (5.3GB); output_bytes_written = 1,080,905 bytes (1.05MB); output_records_written = 1,748; per-batch shuffle ~147MB (confirmed in stage events: shuffle.write.bytesWritten ~146.5MB repeatedly); stage descriptions show 246,796 input records per batch scanned from parquet cache; parquetCacheDiskUsage ~1.8GB stable across all observed stages
agent_insights.suggested_action: Persist or broadcast the large reference/lookup table that is being re-scanned every micro-batch. If it fits in memory (~267MB managed storage used), calling `.cache()` or `.persist()` on it before the streaming query starts would eliminate the repeated parquet scans. If it's a static dimension table, consider using a batch-join pattern (foreachBatch + static DataFrame) instead of joining inside the stream. Also review whether all 67 shuffle partitions are necessary given the single executor — reducing to a smaller number would cut task scheduling overhead.

agent_insights.identifier: Executor off-heap memory fully saturated (100% utilisation) with no explicit overhead configuration
agent_insights.title: Executor off-heap memory fully saturated (100% utilisation) with no explicit overhead configuration
agent_insights.description: The executor's off-heap memory reached 100% utilisation (1.28GB used out of the allocated off-heap budget). `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` is not explicitly configured, so the runtime is using the default of max(384MB, 10% of executor.memory). With executor.memory = ~9.5GB (r6gd.large), the default overhead is ~950MB, but the observed off-heap used is 1.28GB — meaning the process is operating at or above its off-heap ceiling. On Databricks/Spark on YARN/K8s, exhausting off-heap overhead causes the OS to kill the executor container without a clean JVM OOM, making failures hard to diagnose. The risk is currently masked by the small data volume per batch, but any increase in the reference table scan size or concurrent shuffle buffers could tip this into executor death.
agent_insights.evidence: executor_max_off_heap_memory_utilization = 1.0 (100%); executor_max_off_heap_used_memory = 1.28GB; spark.executor.memoryOverhead source = 'not_set'; executor_memory = 9.53GB; default overhead threshold = max(384MB, 9.53GB × 10%) ≈ 953MB; observed usage 1.28GB > estimated default allocation
agent_insights.suggested_action: Explicitly set `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` to at least 1536m (1.5GB) to give the off-heap region headroom above the observed peak of 1.28GB. On Databricks, this is set in the cluster's Spark config. Monitor `executor_max_off_heap_used_memory` across runs to track whether usage is growing with data volume.

triage_result.reasoning:
Reviewing each insight against the triage rules and confirmed metrics:

**Insight 2 — Off-heap memory fully saturated (off_heap_headroom = 0.0):** The metrics confirm `executor_max_off_heap_memory_utilization = 1.0` (100%), meaning zero headroom on off-heap. The triage rule for Tier 1 is `memory_headroom < 0.05` covering heap, but the off-heap dimension (reported as `off_heap_headroom: 0.0` in the snapshot) maps directly to the "Tight heap headroom" spirit — exhausting off-heap overhead causes silent OS-level executor kills. This is a health/correctness risk even if it hasn't triggered a failure yet in this run. Classified Tier 1.

**Insight 3 — Anomalously short run duration (possible incomplete processing):** The run is confirmed at z-score = -1,530, percentile = 0.0 vs a rock-solid historical baseline (std = 18s). This indicates either data skipping, a checkpoint reset, or genuinely incomplete processing. This is a correctness concern — downstream tables may be incomplete. This is a health/correctness issue, Tier 1.

**Insight 0 — commitBatch dominates batch latency:** The Delta checkpoint/WAL commit phase is ~4.3× more expensive than the actual compute work, accounting for ~75% of each batch's wall time. This is a structural performance problem (streaming coordination overhead), not a resource sizing problem. It is the primary driver of batch latency and throughput degradation. No cluster right-sizing or instance type change will fix this — it requires architectural changes (e.g., reducing checkpoint frequency, optimising Delta log writes, caching the reference table). This is a tuning/architectural issue — Tier 4.

**Insight 1 — Massive shuffle-to-output amplification (5,000:1 ratio):** The reference table (~247K rows) is being re-scanned and re-shuffled every micro-batch with no broadcast or caching. vcore_utilization is 0.016 (1.6%), confirming the job is highly CPU-underutilised and mostly spending time on shuffle/IO coordination. The 67-task fan-out stage runs sequentially on a single executor with 2 vCores. This is a query/data pipeline design issue — the fix is caching the reference dataset or using broadcast join. No cluster sizing change addresses this. This is fine-tuning/architectural — Tier 4. Note: AQE status was not explicitly set but shuffle_partitions_param = 'auto' suggests AQE may be active; regardless the recommendation is not about partition count but about caching.

**Conflicts:** Insight 1 (shuffle amplification) and Insight 0 (commitBatch latency) are both Tier 4 but are complementary rather than conflicting — fixing the shuffle (caching the reference table) would reduce per-batch compute time and potentially reduce the delta log commit overhead as well. No conflicts between insights exist. The off-heap saturation fix (insight 2, Tier 1) is not in conflict with any other recommendation; increasing `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` does not conflict with the shuffle or commit-phase recommendations.

tier1.title: Current run duration is anomalously short vs historical baseline — possible incomplete processing
tier1.description: This run completed in 15,721 seconds (4.4 hours), which is an extreme outlier relative to the historical baseline of 43,217 ± 18 seconds (~12 hours) across the 5 prior runs (z-score = -1,530, percentile = 0.0, band = anomalously_low). The historical runs are extraordinarily consistent (std = 18s, <0.1% CV), suggesting they all process the same fixed volume of backlog. The current run processing only 35 batches and 1,748 rows in 4.4 hours — versus the baseline implying ~3× more work at the same batch rate — suggests the stream may have started mid-window, caught up on a smaller backlog, or a checkpoint was reset. This is worth validating: if the short run skipped data, downstream tables may be incomplete.

Confirm that the output table `prod_data_platform_query.payment_form_success` contains the expected row count for the run's time window. If upstream source data volume was genuinely lower, no action is needed, but the anomaly should be flagged in monitoring.

tier4.identifier: Streaming commitBatch dominates batch latency — Delta checkpoint writes are the bottleneck
tier4.title: Streaming commitBatch dominates batch latency — Delta checkpoint writes are the bottleneck
tier4.description: In each micro-batch, the `commitBatch` phase accounts for an average of 15,110ms vs only 3,537ms for `addBatch` (the actual data processing). The commit phase is ~4.3× more expensive than the compute work. This indicates that Delta Lake checkpoint/WAL commit operations — writing offsets and transaction logs — are the rate-limiting step for this streaming query, not CPU or shuffle. With 35 batches over 4.4 hours (avg ~450s/batch), roughly 75% of each batch's wall time is spent on coordination overhead rather than processing. This pattern is exacerbated by the extremely low throughput (0.055 rows/sec input, 1,748 total output rows), meaning the per-row overhead of Delta commits is enormous relative to the data volume processed.
tier4.evidence: batch_operation_duration.commitBatch avg = 15,109ms; batch_operation_duration.addBatch avg = 3,537ms; batch_count = 35 batches over 15,721s total duration; output_records_written = 1,748 rows; processed_rows_per_sec = 2.73 rows/sec overall; trigger_count = 66
tier4.suggested_action: Increase the streaming trigger interval (e.g. set `processingTime` trigger to '5 minutes' or '10 minutes') to amortise the fixed Delta commit cost over more rows per batch. Alternatively, investigate whether the Delta checkpoint location is on a high-latency path (e.g. S3 with many small files) and consider enabling `delta.checkpointInterval` tuning. If the low row volume is permanent, evaluate whether a batch job on a schedule would be more cost-efficient than a continuous stream.

tier4.identifier: Massive shuffle-to-output amplification: 5.3GB shuffle to produce 1.05MB output
tier4.title: Massive shuffle-to-output amplification: 5.3GB shuffle to produce 1.05MB output
tier4.description: Each micro-batch reads ~247K records from a large reference/lookup table and shuffles ~147MB per batch (across 35 batches = ~5.3GB total shuffle) to ultimately write only 1,748 output rows (1.05MB). The shuffle:output ratio is approximately 5,000:1. Stage events show every batch executes a 5-task stage scanning ~247K parquet records via `HashPartitioning(coalesce(add_path_canonical, remove_path_canonical))` followed by a 67-task fan-out stage. The reference dataset (~247K rows, ~1.8GB parquet cache) is being re-scanned and re-shuffled from scratch on every micro-batch rather than being cached or broadcast. With only 2 vCores available and one executor, executing 67 tasks sequentially per batch is also highly serialised.
tier4.evidence: shuffle_bytes_read = 5,276,500,518 bytes (5.3GB); output_bytes_written = 1,080,905 bytes (1.05MB); output_records_written = 1,748; per-batch shuffle ~147MB (confirmed in stage events: shuffle.write.bytesWritten ~146.5MB repeatedly); stage descriptions show 246,796 input records per batch scanned from parquet cache; parquetCacheDiskUsage ~1.8GB stable across all observed stages
tier4.suggested_action: Persist or broadcast the large reference/lookup table that is being re-scanned every micro-batch. If it fits in memory (~267MB managed storage used), calling `.cache()` or `.persist()` on it before the streaming query starts would eliminate the repeated parquet scans. If it's a static dimension table, consider using a batch-join pattern (foreachBatch + static DataFrame) instead of joining inside the stream. Also review whether all 67 shuffle partitions are necessary given the single executor — reducing to a smaller number would cut task scheduling overhead.
